title: Professor Helen X. H. Bao
notes:
Moodle version of Week 6, built on 2026-10-26 from the Week 1 Moodle deck as the format template, in the way Weeks 2, 3, 4, 5 and 7 were built. 18 slides against the 30 asked for. The earlier 70-slide deck is kept beside it (RE07 Week 6 - Performance and Valuation.pptx) as the source of material; it is untouched and describes the earlier shape of the week, nine blocks around the appraisal frame, the cash-flow model, debt sizing, cover ratios, sensitivity analysis, forecasting bias, benchmarking and appraisal smoothing, and a fund manager's hour.

SHAPE OF THE DECK

The first hour is broad and the second hour zooms in. The survey (slides 3 to 8) has four parts, each anchored in a paper or a report whose pages I read: forecasts and the base case (1 slide, traffic forecasts on toll roads), the measurement of fund performance (2 slides, the measures and the evidence on private equity), discount rates in regulated assets (1 slide, the CMA's determination for water) and data centres (2 slides, the beta of listed data-centre property companies and the useful lives of servers). The focus part (slides 9 to 16) takes one question, how to measure the performance and the value of an asset that does not trade, through three models with an interactive page each: the public market equivalent and the direct alpha (Kaplan and Schoar, 2005; Gredil, Griffiths and Stucke), smoothed returns (Getmansky, Lo and Makarov, 2004) and the discount rate built from listed comparators (the CMA's 2026 determination as the worked example, with Ang, Papanikolaou and Westerfield, 2013, on illiquidity). The pages open on generic settings. Then the case (1 slide, headings only) and the summary. There is no thank-you slide.

NO CASE IS CONFIRMED FOR THIS WEEK

Humbert Pang, Managing Principal of Gaw Capital, has agreed to serve on the Panel and has the Week 6 case hour (26 February 2027), moved from Week 3 on 2026-10-19. The note on him records that he has not been told of the move and that he uses WeChat only. No topic is agreed. The first hour is therefore broad and the three focus models are general: each is a test that any real investment, fund or valuation can be put to. The case slide lists kinds of evidence, not a case.

DATA CENTRES

The week's aspect of the course thread on data centres is performance and valuation: the market beta of listed data-centre property companies, which rose from about 0.5 to about 1 (slide 7), and the lives over which servers are depreciated, which hyperscalers moved in opposite directions in 2025 (slide 8). Week 1 slide 27 and Week 3 slides 6 and 7 are not repeated. The beta feeds the third focus model directly (slides 14 and 15), and the useful-life point is a valuation question that the case could test.

WHERE THE EARLIER DECK'S MATERIAL WENT

Blocks A and B (old slides 4 to 17, the four questions of appraisal and the cash-flow model) are not carried: the project cash-flow model belongs to Week 4 and the investor's side of appraisal to Week 2. Block C (old 19 to 24, debt sizing and the cost of equity of a project company) and block D (old 26 to 34, cover ratios) are compressed to a pointer, since Week 4 covers debt sizing, the debt service cover ratio and guarantees; the one idea kept is the cost of equity, which is now the third focus model (old 23 on the cost of equity of a project company is slides 14 and 15). Block E (old 36 to 40, sensitivity, scenarios and Monte Carlo) is dropped, with the old slides in the earlier deck. Block F (old 42 to 50, cost and demand forecasts, reference class forecasting) is compressed to slide 3, since Week 1 covers the iron law of megaproject management and the forecast errors; the old coursework exercise (old 46) is withdrawn with the coursework. Block G (old 52 to 60, benchmarking, wider impacts, levelised cost, appraisal smoothing) is replaced by slides 4, 5, 12 and 13, and old slide 57 on appraisal smoothing is the first of the three models, now with its source. Block H (old 62 to 65, why the applied hour comes from a fund manager) is replaced by the case slide. Block I (old 66 to 70, the reserve) is dropped.

PAGE NUMBERS AND WHAT IS NOT VERIFIED

Every source is cited in the notes of its slide with page numbers, which are the printed page numbers of the version I read; each note states the offset. Several are working papers: Kaplan and Schoar is the NBER conference draft of 6 April 2003 (published in the Journal of Finance 60(4), 2005; I could not retrieve the published article, so its numbers, notably the average PME of 0.80 and 0.91, are the draft's and may differ); Harris, Jenkinson and Kaplan is NBER Working Paper 17874 of February 2012 (Journal of Finance 69(5), 2014); Getmansky, Lo and Makarov is NBER Working Paper 9571 of March 2003 (Journal of Financial Economics 74(3), 2004); Ang, Papanikolaou and Westerfield is NBER Working Paper 19436 of September 2013 (published in Management Science, which I recall and did not check); Van Nieuwerburgh is NBER Working Paper 35865 of October 2026, and the copy of the September conference draft in the vault has different pagination. Lemp and Kockelman is the pre-print of the Transportation Research Record paper (2009); the Standard & Poor's studies it summarises, by Bain and others, were not retrieved. The direct alpha of Gredil, Griffiths and Stucke I know only from two secondary descriptions (a CFA Institute blog and a glossary); the paper was not read. Brown, Ghysels and Gredil (2023) is known only from search summaries. The CMA figures are from a consultancy note (Oxera, 27 March 2026), not from the CMA's own report. The useful-life changes are from Meta's and Amazon's quarterly reports to the SEC for the second quarter of 2025, read by fetch; Alphabet's and Microsoft's changes are in the notes as search summaries only. The values read from Van Nieuwerburgh's Figure 3 are by eye.

Spoken: 'The first hour is a map of how performance and value are measured when an asset does not trade, and where the numbers can mislead. The middle of the hour is three models, each with a page you can run: whether a fund beat the market, whether its reported returns can be believed, and what rate to discount at. Then you meet one principal and we ask what each of the three says about a real portfolio.'

title: Traffic Forecasts and Ramp-Up
notes:
THE FIGURE

Left panel: actual traffic in the first year of operation as a share of the forecast, for new toll roads, by the risk class assigned by Standard & Poor's Traffic Risk Index and by who commissioned the forecast. Low risk 0.90 for forecasts commissioned by banks and 0.80 for those commissioned by others; average risk 0.80 and 0.65; high risk 0.70 and 0.45 (Lemp and Kockelman, 2009, page 3, summarising Bain and Wilkins, 2002). Right panel: the level reached after the ramp-up period as a share of the forecast, for the two classes where the text gives it: average risk about 95 per cent for bank-commissioned and 90 per cent for others, after about five years; high risk about 90 and 80 per cent after about eight years (page 3, continued on page 4). The text gives a ramp-up of about two years for low-risk projects, after which volumes track the forecast on average, and no final level.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The average first-year ratio of actual to forecast traffic was about 0.73 in the first study, of 32 projects, and 0.74, 0.76 and 0.77 in the studies of 2003, 2004 and 2005 (page 2); the samples grew to 68 and 87 projects in the second and third. In the 2002 study 78 per cent of ratios were below 0.9 and only 12 per cent above 1.05, and in the 2003 study 63 per cent were below 0.85; the authors summarise that about three quarters of first-year forecasts for tolled facilities were overestimated by 10 per cent or more (page 3). The riskier the project, the larger the first-year error, the longer the ramp-up and the lower the level it settles at. Forecasts commissioned by banks erred less than those commissioned by others, which the authors link to banks' accountability for investors' money and to other commissioners' interest in high forecasts (page 4). In countries with a history of tolling the first-year ratio averaged 0.81 and elsewhere 0.58 (Bain and Plantagie, 2003, page 4). Compared with non-tolled roads (Flyvbjerg and others), the spread of errors is similar and the tolled distribution is shifted left by about 0.2, a 20 per cent optimism bias (page 4).

WHY IT BELONGS IN THIS WEEK

Every figure in the performance and valuation of a project rests on the base case, and the base case inherits this bias. A cover ratio computed on a forecast that is 25 per cent too high describes a project that does not exist, which is the subject of Week 4 (debt sizing and the debt service cover ratio). The slide is the pointer from this week to that one, and to the Week 1 evidence on the iron law of megaproject management; it is deliberately a single slide.

CAUTIONS

The text I read is the pre-print of the Transportation Research Record paper (Lemp and Kockelman, 2009, volume 2132, pages 106 to 112), and its page numbers are the pre-print's. The Standard & Poor's studies are cited second hand; I could not retrieve them, nor the Fitch Ratings studies the paper also summarises. The ratios are averages of ratios, which bias the average upwards, as the authors note in footnote 1 on page 2: a volume-weighted average would be a more robust indicator, so the true average over-prediction may exceed 33 per cent. The sample is toll roads from around the world over an unstated period, not infrastructure in general. The right panel's figures are the text's approximations ('about').

SOURCE

Lemp, J. D. and Kockelman, K. M. (2009), Understanding and accommodating risk and uncertainty in toll road projects: a review of the literature, pre-print of Transportation Research Record 2132, 106 to 112; pages 2 to 4. Bain, R. and Wilkins, J. (2002) and Bain, R. and Plantagie, J. W. (2003, 2004), Standard & Poor's, as reported there.

A CASE COULD SUPPLY

The forecast of demand or revenue on which the principal's last financing was sized, the first years' outturn against it, and who commissioned the forecast.
text: Traffic Forecasts and Ramp-Up 4 The record: first-year traffic on new toll roads averaged 0.73 to 0.77 of forecast in four Standard & Poor's studies Where it bites: about three quarters of first-year forecasts were overestimated by 10 per cent or more Ramp-up: two years for low-risk projects, five for average and eight for high-risk, with the last two settling below forecast Who commissioned it: forecasts ordered by banks erred less than those ordered by others, 0.80 against 0.65 for average-risk projects Lemp and Kockelman (2009), pre-print of Transportation Research Record 2132, pages 2 to 4, summarising Bain and Wilkins (2002) and later Standard & Poor's studies of 32, 68 and 87 toll roads.

title: Measures of Fund Performance
notes:
THE TABLE

Four measures of the performance of an unlisted fund, with what each states and what it leaves out.

The internal rate of return is the annual rate that sets the discounted net cash flows of the fund to zero. It is what funds report, and the Venture Economics data Kaplan and Schoar used collect it quarterly from the funds (Kaplan and Schoar, 2003 draft, page 5). It does not say what the money could have earned elsewhere, and for a fund that has not been wound up it depends on the manager's estimate of the remaining value.

The multiple of invested capital (the TVPI of the data sets) is total distributions plus the remaining value per unit contributed. In the Venture Economics sample the average fund returned roughly twice the capital committed (page 10). It ignores timing: a multiple of 1.8 over five years and over fifteen are the same number.

The public market equivalent discounts the fund's distributions and contributions, all net of fees, at the total return on an index, and divides: above one means the fund outperformed (page 9 of the draft). Harris, Jenkinson and Kaplan describe it as a market-adjusted multiple of invested capital: a PME of 1.20 means that investors ended up with 20 per cent more than if they had invested in the public market (page 10 of the working paper, printed page).

The direct alpha is the internal rate of return of the cash flows after each has been compounded to the end date at the index's return, which gives an annual excess return over the index. On the descriptions I could find, it is the annualised form of the Kaplan and Schoar ratio and gives the same verdict, positive when the ratio is above one; one glossary notes that the paper defines it in continuously compounded form while its examples report a discrete rate, so it should be labelled when reported.

THE POINT

The first two measures ignore the benchmark and the last two need one. The choice of benchmark is therefore the substantive judgement in any statement that a fund outperformed. Kaplan and Schoar note that if the fund's market beta is above one the ratio overstates risk-adjusted performance (page 9 of the draft).

CAUTIONS

Kaplan and Schoar's paper was read as the NBER conference draft of 6 April 2003 (the published version is Journal of Finance 60(4), 2005), whose pagination is the draft's, and Harris, Jenkinson and Kaplan as NBER Working Paper 17874 of February 2012 (Journal of Finance 69(5), 2014), where the printed page is the PDF page less two. The direct alpha is the paper of Gredil, Griffiths and Stucke (a 2014 working paper, published in the Journal of Corporate Finance in 2023 according to one glossary), which I did not retrieve: the description is from the CFA Institute Enterprising Investor blog of 23 July 2014 and the Altss glossary. Nothing on this slide rests on the paper's own text.

SOURCE

Kaplan, S. N. and Schoar, A. (2003 draft; 2005), Private equity performance: returns, persistence and capital flows, pages 9 and 10; Harris, R. S., Jenkinson, T. and Kaplan, S. N. (2012; 2014), Private equity performance: what do we know?, page 10; Gredil, O., Griffiths, B. and Stucke, R., Benchmarking private equity: the direct alpha method, as described in secondary sources.

A CASE COULD SUPPLY

Which of the four measures the principal reports to its investors and uses internally, the benchmark in use, and the date at which the last unrealised value was struck.
text: Measures of Fund Performance 4 Kaplan and Schoar (2005), NBER conference draft of 6 April 2003, pages 9 and 10; Harris, Jenkinson and Kaplan (2012), NBER Working Paper 17874, page 10; Gredil, Griffiths and Stucke (2014 working paper) as described in secondary sources. Measure What it states What it leaves out Internal rate of return The annual rate that sets the discounted net cash flows to zero What the money could have earned elsewhere; the manager's estimate of any remaining value Multiple of invested capital Distributions plus remaining value for each unit contributed Timing: a multiple of 1.8 over five years and over fifteen is the same number Public market equivalent Value of distributions relative to value of contributions, both compounded at an index (Kaplan and Schoar) The choice of index and its beta; a ratio and not a rate Direct alpha The internal rate of return of the index-compounded flows, an annual excess return (Gredil, Griffiths and Stucke) The same dependence on the benchmark; the paper itself was not read

title: Private Equity Performance across Data Sets and Benchmarks
notes:
THE FIGURE

Average public market equivalent of private equity funds in two studies. The two lighter bars are from Kaplan and Schoar's draft of April 2003, which used Venture Economics data on 776 funds with largely complete cash flows: for all private equity funds, the equal-weighted average PME was 0.80 (median 0.65) and the commitment-weighted average 0.91 (median 0.80), against the S&P 500 (page 10 of the draft, Table 2, text). The darker bars are from Harris, Jenkinson and Kaplan (2012), who used Burgiss cash-flow data on U.S. buyout funds of vintages 1984 to 2008: the sample average PME was 1.20 against the S&P 500, 1.18 against the Russell 3000, 1.17 against the Nasdaq, 1.11 against the Russell 2000 and 1.07 against the Russell 2000 Value (page 19, printed, text on Table 6).

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The two studies reach opposite verdicts, and the difference is not a matter of method, since both use the same measure. Kaplan and Schoar found that private equity had not returned as much as the S&P 500 (page 10 of the draft). Harris, Jenkinson and Kaplan, with Burgiss data, find buyout PMEs consistently above one: the average of the weighted vintage PMEs is 1.27, of the vintage averages 1.22 and of the medians 1.16, which imply outperformance of 20 to 27 per cent over a fund's life, and more than 3 per cent a year (page 16 of the working paper, printed, and the abstract). They attribute part of the difference to the data: they say that their own results and Stucke (2011) provide strong evidence that Venture Economics, and hence Kaplan and Schoar, understate the returns of 1980s and 1990s vintage funds (page 17). The sample also differs, since Kaplan and Schoar's covers venture and buyout funds together and the later study's buyout funds are shown here, and the periods differ (funds raised before 1997 against vintages to 2008). For venture capital the later study finds PMEs above one for most of the 1990s and below one for the 1999 to 2002 vintages (page 18). The choice of benchmark moves the buyout figure from 1.20 to 1.07, still above one, which the authors read as consistent with buyout funds having value characteristics (page 19).

THE LESSON

A public market equivalent is a statement about a data set, a period and a benchmark, as much as about a fund. The numbers cannot be compared across studies without those three.

CAUTIONS

The figures for Kaplan and Schoar are the draft's: the published article may differ. The bars mix different samples and are not the same funds. The Burgiss PMEs are conditional on the valuations of unrealised investments, which the authors say they take to be reasonable after the accounting rule (Topic 820) that tightened fair-value measurement; most 2000s vintages were not yet fully realised. The study is about United States funds, not infrastructure.

SOURCE

Kaplan, S. N. and Schoar, A. (2003 draft), page 10; Harris, R. S., Jenkinson, T. and Kaplan, S. N. (2012), NBER Working Paper 17874, pages 16 to 19 (printed pages; PDF page less two).

A CASE COULD SUPPLY

The principal's own PME or direct alpha for its funds or assets, with the index and the vintage, and the share of value still unrealised.
text: Private Equity Performance across Data Sets and Benchmarks 4 Early data: using Venture Economics data, the average private equity fund earned 0.80 of what the S&P 500 would have (0.91 weighting by commitment) Later data: Burgiss cash flows give U.S. buyout funds an average of 1.20, an outperformance of 20 to 27 per cent over a fund's life The benchmark: the buyout figure falls from 1.20 against the S&P 500 to 1.07 against small-cap value, still above one Venture capital: above one for most 1990s vintages and below one for the 1999 to 2002 vintages Kaplan and Schoar (2005), NBER conference draft of 6 April 2003, page 10 (Venture Economics, 776 funds); Harris, Jenkinson and Kaplan (2012), NBER Working Paper 17874, pages 16 to 19 (Burgiss, U.S. buyout funds). Different samples and periods.

title: Allowed Returns in Regulated Water
notes:
THE TABLE

Table 2.1 of Oxera's note of 27 March 2026 on the Competition and Markets Authority's (CMA) final determinations of Ofwat's PR24 price review for five water companies, in CPIH-real terms. Market data cut-off 30 September 2024 for Ofwat's final determination (FD), 30 June 2025 for the CMA's provisional findings (PF) and 30 November 2025 for the CMA's FD. Gearing 55 per cent in all three. Risk-free rate 1.52, 2.49 and 2.40 per cent. Equity beta 0.59 to 0.65 (Ofwat), 0.61 to 0.76 with a point estimate of 0.68 (PF) and 0.61 to 0.70 with a point of 0.66 (CMA FD). Total market return 6.68 to 6.98 per cent, 6.70 to 7.30 (point 7.00) and 6.70 to 7.20 (point 6.95). Return on equity, point estimates, 5.10, 5.90 and 5.70 per cent. Return on debt 3.15, 2.98 and 2.97 per cent. Appointee weighted average cost of capital 4.03, 4.29 and 4.20 per cent; on the wholesale basis 3.97, 4.29 and 4.20.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Three regulatory decisions on the same companies, the same year, with the same method (the capital asset pricing model, consistently with Ofwat), give weighted costs that differ by up to 26 basis points, and the differences come from the inputs and the date. The CMA raised the return on equity by 60 basis points over Ofwat's (5.70 against 5.10) and, with changes to the allowed return on debt, the wholesale weighted cost by 23 basis points (4.20 against 3.97; 17 basis points on the appointee basis). Oxera's note identifies two methodological changes of the CMA: a different source of swap data for the swap wedge adjustment to the risk-free rate, which cut that adjustment by about 17 basis points, and the inclusion of Pennon as a beta comparator from 1 October 2021 (page 2). The beta ranges are built from three listed water companies, Severn Trent, United Utilities and Pennon, over three and ten years of daily returns (section 2.1, page 4). The point of the slide is that even the one setting where a price is fixed by an authority, a discount rate for a long-lived regulated asset is a judgement about a beta and a date.

THE BRIDGE TO THE FOCUS PART

The third model builds a discount rate from a listed comparator in the same way, with the CMA's inputs as a preset, and shows what a rate does to value (slides 14 and 15).

CAUTIONS

The source is a consultancy note summarising the CMA's published determination; I did not read the CMA's report (Water PR24 references: final determinations, volume 4, chapter 7). Oxera's table shows a point estimate for Ofwat's return on equity (5.10) that lies above the top of the range printed for it (4.58 to 5.07); I report it as extracted from the PDF, which should be checked against the PDF. The figures are CPIH-real and for water; other regulators use other bases (the Civil Aviation Authority's H8 decision for Heathrow, which I could not retrieve, is not used here). The note's cut-off dates are the dates of the market data, not of publication.

SOURCE

Oxera (27 March 2026), CMA PR24 water redeterminations, section 2, Table 2.1 on page 2, the bridge in Figure 2.1 on page 3 and section 2.1 on page 4. Competition and Markets Authority (10 March 2026), Final Determinations, Volume 4, Chapter 7, as cited there and not read.

A CASE COULD SUPPLY

The discount rate or required return the principal uses for an asset or a bid, how it was built, and who signed it off.

title: Data-Centre Betas
notes:
THE FIGURE

Approximate readings of the rolling 36-month beta of listed data-centre property companies' returns on the excess return of the S&P 500, from Figure 3 of Van Nieuwerburgh (2026), which plots the line monthly from early 2021 (the window needs 36 months, and the sample starts in January 2018) to March 2026. The control variables are the 10-year Treasury return and the Fama-French size, value, profitability and investment factors; the dependent variable is the value-weighted return on data-centre REITs from the FTSE Nareit U.S. Real Estate Index Series, minus the Treasury bill rate (page 14, notes to the figure). The bars are my readings of the black line at the start of each year: about 0.55 in early 2021, 0.53 in early 2022, 0.54 in early 2023, 0.92 in early 2024, 0.97 in early 2025 and about 1.0 in early 2026, and about 0.55 at the last observation, March 2026. They are read by eye from a printed chart and are accurate to about 0.05; I did not have the underlying data.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The text says that the market beta of publicly traded data-centre REITs has risen from roughly 0.5 to around 1, indicating that their returns now move much more closely with the broader equity market, and that their exposure to the non-AI component of the S&P 500 has also risen and is now comparable to their exposure to AI stocks (page 13). The author concludes that data centres appear less like defensive infrastructure assets or a hedge against AI-related risk and more like part of the same systematic risk complex (page 13). The figure shows the final observation falling back to about 0.55, which the text does not discuss; it is a single point of a rolling estimate and I have not tried to explain it. The effect on valuation is shown in slide 15: with the same other inputs, a comparator beta of 0.5 gives a weighted cost of capital of 6.35 per cent and a beta of 1.0 gives 8.10 per cent, and the value of a 25-year cash flow growing at 2 per cent is 16 per cent lower.

THE RISKS BEHIND IT

The paper names three vulnerabilities: concentration in tenants and end demand, technological obsolescence, and execution, financed with high asset-level leverage and layered claims (pages 12 and 13). It also estimates that the 2025 to 2032 buildout needs about $3.55 trillion a year of mature revenue to earn a 10 per cent unlevered return at a 50 per cent operating cash-flow margin, equal to about 8.8 per cent of 2032 GDP, $5.1 per installed GB300 GPU-hour at full utilisation or $6.4 per billed GPU-hour at 80 per cent utilisation, comparable with frontier GPU rental prices at the end of August 2026 (page 12). That is the valuation question in one line: whether the cash flows can reach the level at which the assets earn their cost of capital.

CAUTIONS

Van Nieuwerburgh's paper is NBER Working Paper 35865 of October 2026, forthcoming in Brookings Papers on Economic Activity; the page numbers are the printed ones of that version, and the copy of the 4 September conference draft in Resources/Week 2 has different pagination. The beta is a regression estimate on listed REITs, which own leased buildings rather than the hyperscalers' own campuses; it is a comparator for a leased data-centre asset and not for a chip-heavy one. It is a three-year window that moves slowly by construction. The readings are mine, from the figure.

SOURCE

Van Nieuwerburgh, S. (2026), Financing the AI buildout, NBER Working Paper 35865; text on page 13, Figure 3 on page 14, revenue arithmetic on page 12.

A CASE COULD SUPPLY

The beta, the cap rate or the discount rate the principal uses for a data-centre or digital asset, and the comparators it chose.

Values read by eye from the figure, accurate to about 0.05.

title: Asset Lives and Reported Earnings in Data Centres
notes:
THE TABLE

Two hyperscalers' changes to the useful life over which servers and network equipment are depreciated, effective 1 January 2025, with the stated effects for the first half of 2025.

Meta Platforms: in January 2025 it completed an assessment of the useful lives of property and equipment, which increased the estimated useful lives of most servers and network assets to 5.5 years, effective 1 January 2025 (Note 1, Use of estimates, Form 10-Q for the quarter ended 30 June 2025). For the six months ended 30 June 2025 the change reduced depreciation expense by $1.58 billion and raised net income by $1.34 billion, or $0.52 per diluted share (same note). Its annual report for 2025 describes the same change under critical accounting estimates, and lists servers and network assets at five to 5.5 years, against four to five years in the 2024 annual report (as shown by search summaries of the filings; I read only the MD&A passage of the 2025 report).

Amazon: effective 1 January 2025 it shortened the useful life of a subset of its servers and networking equipment from six years to five years, which it attributes to the faster pace of technology development, particularly in AI and machine learning (Note 1, Use of estimates, Form 10-Q for the quarter ended 30 June 2025). For the second quarter the change was an increase in depreciation and amortisation of $280 million and a reduction in net income of $217 million; for the six months, an increase of $497 million and a reduction of $379 million, or $0.04 per share (same note). The change primarily affected AWS.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Two large operators looking at similar equipment in the same year moved their depreciation lives in opposite directions, one lengthening and one shortening, and each move had an effect on reported profit that is large against the quarter's earnings. Depreciation life is the accounting expression of the economic life that a valuer has to forecast, and a lender or a landlord of a data centre faces the same question over the asset's residual value. Van Nieuwerburgh (2026) names obsolescence as the second vulnerability of the buildout: campuses built around current chip generations may become less competitive well before their structures wear out, and rising rack densities, new interconnect standards and changing cooling requirements can require costly retrofits, creating a mismatch between the long maturity of infrastructure financing and the potentially much shorter economic life of the assets (page 12). On the valuation question he writes that AI infrastructure combines long-lived buildings and power systems with hardware whose economic life may be much shorter and more uncertain, which raises questions about depreciation, collateral values, lease duration, refinancing risk and the maturity of debt (page 15), and that capacity commissioned in 2025 and 2026 may need substantial GPU replacement by about 2030, while buildings and power infrastructure remain usable (page 24). In the Hyperion financing of Week 4 the lender's protection against the residual value is a guarantee from the tenant: Meta must cover any shortfall between the sale proceeds and a contractually specified minimum value if it ends the lease (page 9, printed).

WHAT THE MARKET SAYS ABOUT THE BUILDING

CBRE's North America Data Center Trends report for the first half of 2026, as I could read it on its web page, gives vacancy of 1.4 per cent, asking rents up 8.3 per cent for 3 to 10 megawatt requirements and 80.4 per cent of capacity under construction already pre-leased. I did not find cap rates or valuation yields in the pages I could read, nor a peer-reviewed estimate of the economic life of a data-centre shell or of a GPU, so the slide offers none.

CAUTIONS

Meta's figures are from the Form 10-Q I read for the June 2025 quarter; Amazon's too. title: Measuring an Asset That Does Not Trade
notes:
THE LIST

The focus part takes one question, how to measure the performance and the value of an asset that does not trade, and three models of it. An unlisted asset has no price series, so a return has to be inferred from cash flows and a few valuations, and a value from a discount rate. The three models correspond to the three inferences. Each has a page that can be run, and each comes with a paper whose pages I read.

Model 1 is the public market equivalent of Kaplan and Schoar (2005) and the direct alpha of Gredil, Griffiths and Stucke, which compare a fund's cash flows with what an index would have delivered (slides 10 and 11; pme.html). It corrects the internal rate of return for the opportunity cost of the money.

Model 2 is the smoothing model of Getmansky, Lo and Makarov (2004), in which reported returns average true ones (slides 12 and 13; smoothing.html). It says what valuation lags do to measured risk, Sharpe ratio and beta.

Model 3 is the discount rate built from listed comparators, with the CMA's determination for water as the worked case and the data-centre beta as the live problem (slides 14 and 15; discount.html). It shows what a rate does to value and what an extra premium for illiquidity would do, drawing on Ang, Papanikolaou and Westerfield (2013).

WHY THESE THREE

They are three places where an unlisted asset's number comes from a judgement that cannot be tested against a price: the benchmark, the valuation lag and the discount rate. The slides after them put the three side by side (slide 16) and ask what a real investment would show for each. The first two are about the past, the third is about the future; a valuation by an investor at a point in time needs all three.

OVERLAPS TO NOTE

Week 3 covers the J-curve and fund fees and the evidence of Andonov, Kräussl and Rauh (2021) on infrastructure fund performance; this week does not repeat them and its measures are what they would be assessed with. Week 5's model on the illiquidity discount in a market with search frictions (Duffie, Gârleanu and Pedersen, 2005) is the theory behind the extra premium in the third model; this week takes the premium as an input.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

Which of the three the principal's own numbers depend on: the benchmark in the reported performance, the lag in its valuations and the rate used to value or bid.
text: Measuring an Asset That Does Not Trade 4 Performance against the market: the public market equivalent and the direct alpha: Kaplan and Schoar (2005); Gredil, Griffiths and Stucke Reported values: the smoothing of appraisal-based returns: Getmansky, Lo and Makarov (2004) Discount rates: the cost of capital of an asset with no traded price: listed comparators, the CMA's determination for water, and the cost of illiquidity The common problem: the asset does not trade, so a return or a value is inferred from cash flows, appraisals or comparators, and each inference has a known bias

title: Kaplan and Schoar (2005): The Public Market Equivalent
notes:
THE FIGURE

A generic fund at the settings of pme.html. One unit of capital is called in each of years 0 to 3, and the fund returns 1.8 times the capital called, in six equal instalments in years 5 to 10, so that the total distributions are 7.2 (left panel, net cash flows). The internal rate of return of these flows is 10.4 per cent a year. The right panel compounds each flow to year 10 at a steady index return of 7 per cent a year, the step that the direct alpha and the public market equivalent have in common. The public market equivalent, the sum of the distributions divided by the sum of the contributions, each at the index's value, is 1.20. The internal rate of return of the compounded flows is 3.2 per cent, which is the direct alpha, and with a steady index it equals (1 plus the fund's internal rate of return) divided by (1 plus the index return) minus one, which I derived and the page checks.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Kaplan and Schoar define the public market equivalent as the discounted value of the fund's cash outflows relative to the discounted value of its cash inflows, all net of fees, where the discounting is at the total return on the S&P 500; this compares investing in the fund with investing in the index, and a fund with a PME greater than one outperformed the index (page 9 of the draft). They do not adjust for risk beyond using the index as the benchmark, because there is no true market value in the early years of a fund's life, and they point out that if private equity returns have a beta greater than one, the PME overstates risk-adjusted returns; Jones and Rhodes-Kropf find betas of 1.11 for venture capital and 0.81 for leveraged buyouts, and Ljungqvist and Richardson about 1.10, and Kaplan and Schoar think these estimates may understate the market risk (page 9). The direct alpha compounds the flows at the index return to a common date and takes the internal rate of return, so that it gives the verdict on the same flows as a rate a year (Gredil, Griffiths and Stucke; description from secondary sources only).

THE CONDITION

The calculation is clean for a fund that has distributed everything. Kaplan and Schoar repeated their analysis on a second sample of 776 funds that were liquidated or whose returns had been unchanged for six quarters and whose unrealised value was below 10 per cent of committed capital, to avoid sensitivity to subjective reporting (page 7). For a live fund the final term is the manager's valuation, which is where the second model (smoothing) comes in.

CAUTIONS

The figure is a stylised fund with flows I chose. The page numbers of Kaplan and Schoar are those of the draft of 6 April 2003. The direct alpha is not from the paper's text; see slide 4.

SOURCE

Kaplan, S. N. and Schoar, A. (2003 draft; 2005), Private equity performance: returns, persistence and capital flows, pages 7 and 9; Gredil, O., Griffiths, B. and Stucke, R., Benchmarking private equity: the direct alpha method, as described in secondary sources. Figure from models_w6.py.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

The principal's own funds' cash flows by date, net of fees, the index it uses to benchmark them, and the value assigned to what remains unrealised.
text: Kaplan and Schoar (2005): The Public Market Equivalent 4 The idea: compound each contribution and each distribution at an index, and compare the value of what came back with the value of what went in The result: a fund with a multiple of 1.8 called over four years and returned over years 5 to 10 has an IRR of 10.4 per cent and, against a steady 7 per cent index, a PME of 1.20 Direct alpha: the same compounded flows give an annual excess return of 3.2 per cent, with the same sign as the PME The condition: the fund must be fully realised, or its last reported value stands in for a sale Kaplan and Schoar (2005), NBER conference draft of 6 April 2003, pages 7 and 9; Gredil, Griffiths and Stucke as described in secondary sources. A generic fund, the settings of pme.html; not calibrated to any fund.

title: The Verdict Depends on the Benchmark
notes:
THE FIGURE

The same fund as the previous slide (a multiple of 1.8, called over four years, returned over years 5 to 10) against an index with an average return of 7 per cent and a risk-free rate of 2 per cent, under three paths of the index and two benchmarks. With the index steady at 7 per cent the PME is 1.20. With the index 8 points above its average in the first five years and 8 points below in the second five (gaining early), the PME is 1.12; with the reverse (gaining late) it is 1.35. Scaling the benchmark to a beta of 1.4 (the risk-free rate plus 1.4 times the index's excess return) lowers the steady-index PME to 1.08 and the early-gain figure to 0.98; the direct alpha at a steady index is 1.3 per cent a year against 3.2. The page lets you set all of these.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The same flows give different verdicts depending on when the benchmark gains, because the index has already risen by the time distributions arrive when it gains early, so each distribution is compared with a larger base, and the reverse when it gains late. The benchmark's beta matters in the same direction as Kaplan and Schoar's remark on page 9 of the draft: a fund with a market beta above one looks better against an index with beta one than it would against a benchmark of its own risk. The two parts of the verdict that no formula supplies are the beta and the final value of the fund. Harris, Jenkinson and Kaplan show the same thing across benchmarks and data sets (slide 5, pages 16 to 19 of their working paper), and Brown, Ghysels and Gredil (2023, Review of Financial Studies 36(3), known to me from search summaries only) estimate that the market beta of an average buyout fund is 1.05 to 1.10 and of an average venture fund 1.20 to 1.32 using a model that combines cash flows, reported values and public comparables; I did not read it.

WHAT TO ASK OF ANY STATEMENT THAT A FUND OUTPERFORMED

Which index and which beta, over which dates, net of what fees and how much of the value is unrealised.

CAUTIONS

The generic fund, the index paths and the swing of 8 points are mine; they illustrate a direction and do not estimate an effect. The early and late paths keep the average arithmetic return at 7 per cent, and the compound return differs slightly.

SOURCE

Kaplan, S. N. and Schoar, A. (2003 draft), page 9; Harris, Jenkinson and Kaplan (2012), pages 16 to 19; Brown, G. W., Ghysels, E. and Gredil, O. (2023), Nowcasting net asset values: the case of private equity, Review of Financial Studies 36(3), 945 to 986, from a search summary. Interactive page: web/pme.html.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

The benchmark the principal reports against and whether it is the right risk: ask for the PME or the direct alpha on two benchmarks, and for the date of the last valuation in each fund's final term.

title: Getmansky, Lo and Makarov (2004): Smoothed Returns
notes:
THE FIGURE

Left: the weights of the example, declining over the current and three earlier quarters, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1, which sum to one (page 20, equations 21 to 23). Right: one random path of 40 quarters at the settings of smoothing.html, with true returns of mean 8 per cent and volatility 16 per cent a year, a beta of 0.8 on a market of volatility 16 per cent, drawn with a fixed seed. The reported return in each quarter is the weighted average of that quarter's true return and the previous three. The reported series is flatter, and it moves after the true series does.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Getmansky, Lo and Makarov (2004) model observed returns as a weighted average of true returns over the current period and the last k periods, with weights between zero and one summing to one (equations 21 to 23, pages 19 and 20 of the working paper). The weights sum to one so that the information driving performance is eventually fully reflected in observed returns, but it can take up to k+1 periods (page 21). They explain why reported returns are smooth for illiquid portfolios: infrequent trading, marks extrapolated from the latest transaction price, quotes averaged from dealers, and, less innocently, deliberate performance smoothing (pages 18 and 19); the securities named include real estate and restricted securities. Proposition 1 (equations 24 to 33, page 22) gives the consequences: the expected return is unchanged; the variance is multiplied by the sum of the squared weights, 0.30 in the example, so the volatility is 55 per cent of the true figure; the Sharpe ratio is multiplied by the reciprocal of its square root, 1.83; the contemporaneous beta is the true beta times the weight on the current quarter, 0.32 against a true 0.80; the covariance with the market lagged m quarters is the weight on lag m times the true beta, so the lagged betas add up to the true beta; and the first-order autocorrelation of the reported series is 0.67. The paper's own words are that smoothing biases the market beta towards zero or market neutrality, and gives a formal reading of Asness, Krail and Liew's finding that many hedge funds have significant lagged market exposure despite low contemporaneous betas (page 22).

WHAT SURVIVES

The long-run behaviour. The variance of the return over twenty quarters of the reported series is 95 per cent of the true variance in the example, because the weights sum to one, and the volatility 97 per cent. Smoothing flatters short-horizon risk statistics and leaves the long-horizon ones nearly intact.

CAUTIONS

The paper is about hedge funds and the sample is hedge funds; the extension to infrastructure is mine, with the authors' own examples of real estate and private placements as support (pages 18 and 19). I read the NBER working paper of March 2003; the published article is Journal of Financial Economics 74(3), 2004. The equations in my extracted text were garbled in places, and I checked the formulas against the text of Proposition 1 and by a simulation of 400,000 periods (check_models_w6.py), but the published article should be checked. The weights in the example are mine; the paper estimates them from data.

SOURCE

Getmansky, M., Lo, A. W. and Makarov, I. (2004), An econometric model of serial correlation and illiquidity in hedge fund returns, Journal of Financial Economics 74(3), 529 to 609; NBER Working Paper 9571 (March 2003), pages 18 to 22 (printed page = PDF page less three).

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

The principal's valuation policy: who values the assets, how often, from what, and whether valuations are lagged behind transaction prices; and a quarterly series of its reported returns against a listed index.
text: Getmansky, Lo and Makarov (2004): Smoothed Returns 4 The model: the reported return is a weighted average of the true returns of the current and the last k quarters, with weights summing to one The example: weights of 0.4, 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1 on the current and three earlier quarters The effect: reported volatility is 55 per cent of the true figure, the Sharpe ratio 1.83 times as high, and the same-quarter beta 0.32 against a true 0.80 What survives: the average return and, over five years, nearly all of the volatility (97 per cent of the true figure) Getmansky, Lo and Makarov (2004), NBER Working Paper 9571, pages 18 to 22 (equations 21 to 33). title: Smoothing in Unlisted Infrastructure Indices
notes:
THE FIGURE

Annual volatility and beta against the MSCI World index of the EDHECinfra index of unlisted global infrastructure equity and of eight listed infrastructure indices, from Table 8 of Lambrev (2019), page 35, computed from quarterly data. EDHECinfra: volatility 3.0 per cent, beta 0.04, Sharpe ratio 5.33 and return 15.9 per cent. Listed: DJ Brookfield 14.0 and 0.74; MSCI 13.3 and 0.60; RARE 13.2 and 0.54; S&P 16.5 and 0.69; STOXX 14.1 and 0.63; Macquarie 12.1 and 0.49; FTSE 12.0 and 0.52. MSCI World itself has volatility 15.6 per cent (the beta is not applicable). Sharpe ratios of the listed indices run from 0.10 (MSCI) to 0.69 (FTSE), with a risk-free rate of minus 0.346 per cent (the three-month Euribor on 1 July 2019).

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

An unlisted index of infrastructure equity shows volatility a fifth of the listed ones' and a beta of 0.04, and a Sharpe ratio of 5.33 where equity markets deliver about 0.5. Lambrev reads the comparison as showing that the commonly used listed infrastructure indices misrepresent the characteristics of unlisted infrastructure, and that the listed universe is an ill-defined category that includes companies with little infrastructure business (pages 35 and 36, abstract). The smoothing model gives a second reading, which I did not find tested in the paper: an index built from appraisals and valuations of unlisted assets would be expected to have exactly this signature if the valuation lags the price, and the model says how large the effect would be for a given lag. With the weights of the previous slide the reported volatility would be 55 per cent of the true figure, which is not enough to account for a fifth, so the lag would have to be longer or the weights more concentrated, or the true volatility lower. The model does not decide between the two readings. It says that a volatility of 3 per cent and a beta of 0.04 are not by themselves evidence about the assets.

THE CORRECTION

Desmoothing inverts the assumed updating rule and raises the estimated volatility and beta. The page shows a first-order version that uses the first-order autocorrelation of the reported series and is exact when the smoothing is geometric; for other weights it over-corrects (in the example it gives a volatility 22 per cent above the true figure). The input is an estimate of the lag.

CAUTIONS

Lambrev's text says the data are quarterly from 1 January 2007 to 31 December 2018 (page 24) and that the regression results are as of 30 July 2007, while the abstract and the discussion say 2001 to 2018; I use the table as printed and the discrepancy is not resolved. The EDHECinfra index of 2019 is built on a sampled universe of unlisted companies and is not the index EDHEC publishes now. The paper is published in a regional economics journal, Naše gospodarstvo / Our Economy, 65(3), 23 to 39, and its own regressions are simple. Lambrev uses the Euribor as the risk-free rate, which inflates the Sharpe ratios of all the indices alike.

SOURCE

Lambrev, D. (2019), Infrastructure indices: comparative analysis of performance, risk and representation of global listed proxies, Naše gospodarstvo / Our Economy 65(3), 23 to 39; Table 8 on page 35. Getmansky, Lo and Makarov (2004), page 22. Interactive page: web/smoothing.html.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

A quarterly return series for the principal's unlisted assets next to a listed comparator, and the lag with which its valuations follow transactions.

title: Building a Discount Rate from Listed Comparators
notes:
THE FIGURE

Left: the build-up of the cost of capital for a regulated network at the inputs of the CMA's final determination for water (Oxera, 2026, Table 2.1, page 2): a risk-free rate of 2.40 per cent, an equity beta of 0.66 on a market premium of 4.55 per cent (the total market return of 6.95 per cent less 2.40), which contributes 3.00; a further 0.30 that I add so that the cost of equity equals the CMA's 5.70 per cent (the capital asset pricing model alone gives 5.40); a return on debt of 2.97 per cent; gearing 55 per cent. The weighted cost is 4.20 per cent, the CMA's figure. Right: a listed data-centre comparator at two betas with otherwise generic inputs (risk-free rate 4 per cent, premium 5 per cent, comparator gearing 30 per cent, target gearing 40 per cent, cost of debt 5.5 per cent): a comparator beta of 0.5 gives a cost of equity of 6.92 per cent and a weighted cost of 6.35; a beta of 1.0 gives 9.83 and 8.10.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

An unlisted asset has no share price, so valuers borrow the beta of listed comparators, strip out the effect of their gearing to get an asset beta, put back the gearing the asset will carry, and add the cost of debt weighted by the gearing. The CMA used a capital asset pricing model for the cost of equity, with the risk-free rate from 20-year index-linked gilt yields adjusted to CPIH, the beta from Severn Trent, United Utilities and Pennon over three and ten years of daily returns, and an equity risk premium from the total market return (Oxera, section 2.1, page 4). The inputs are all uncertain and dated, and the slide on regulated returns showed how three regulatory decisions on the same companies differ. The right panel applies the same arithmetic to the problem of slide 7: if the comparator beta is 0.5 the rate is 6.35 per cent, and if it is 1.0 it is 8.10.

ILLIQUIDITY

A valuer may add an extra premium for the cost of not being able to sell. Ang, Papanikolaou and Westerfield (2013) model an investor who cannot trade an asset for intervals of uncertain length. Their abstract states that uncertainty about the length of the interval, as opposed to a deterministic non-trading interval, is a primary determinant of the cost of illiquidity, and that investors are willing to forego 2 per cent of their wealth to hedge against illiquidity crises occurring once every ten years; they also find that for typical parameters an investor would pay 0.5 to 2 per cent a year over the actuarial probability of a crisis to receive liquid funds at the onset of one (page 3). The page treats the premium as an input and does not take a value from the paper. Week 5's model on search and the dealer (Duffie, Gârleanu and Pedersen) is the other theory of the same discount.

A DATED INPUT

The risk-free rate is the input that moves most between the dates of two decisions. The Economist of 16 September 2026 reports that the yield on ten-year American Treasuries exceeded 5 per cent on 14 September, the highest in two decades, and that the median ten-year yield in rich countries was above 4 per cent, its highest in more than 15 years and roughly five times its average in 2015 to 2021; it cites the OECD's estimate that the average term premium had risen by more than one percentage point from its pre-2020 level by the end of 2025. The CMA's risk-free rate of 2.40 per cent is a CPIH-real figure from 20-year index-linked gilts with market data to 30 November 2025, so it is a different quantity from the nominal ten-year yields in the article and the two cannot be compared directly; the point is that a rate dated 2024 or 2025 is stale by the date of a valuation in 2027. I read the article's text from the saved PDF; I did not read its charts, and the yields should be checked before they are quoted.

CAUTIONS

The CMA's own cost of equity involved a choice of point in a range (5.02 to 5.76 per cent), and the capital asset pricing model with the table's point inputs gives about 5.40 rather than 5.70; the extra 0.30 on the slide is my adjustment to reproduce the CMA's figure and is not the CMA's own. The CMA's report was not read. The data-centre inputs other than the beta are generic. The arithmetic ignores tax and the tax shield, and the debt beta is set to zero. The beta values are read by eye from a figure (slide 7). The Ang, Papanikolaou and Westerfield paper is the NBER working paper of September 2013, with printed page = PDF page less one; the published version is Management Science (2014), which I recall and did not check.

SOURCE

Oxera (27 March 2026), pages 2 and 4; Van Nieuwerburgh (2026), Figure 3; Ang, A., Papanikolaou, D. and Westerfield, M. M. (2013), Portfolio choice with illiquid assets, NBER Working Paper 19436, abstract and page 3; The Economist (16 September 2026), Soaring bond yields, gaping deficits and towering debts. Interactive page: web/discount.html.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

The rate at which the principal values or bids for an asset, its comparators and their dates, the gearing assumed, and any premium added for illiquidity; and whether the rate changed when the comparators' betas did.

title: Value as a Function of the Discount Rate
notes:
THE FIGURE

The value of a cash flow of 1 in the first year growing at 2 per cent a year, in units of that first-year cash flow, against the discount rate, for flows of 10, 25 and 50 years and for a flow that never ends (the model's value_multiple; page: discount.html). The two dots are the weighted costs of the data-centre comparator of the previous slide at betas of 0.5 and 1.0: 6.35 per cent, where the 25-year flow is worth 14.9, and 8.10 per cent, where it is worth 12.6.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The value of a long cash flow is very sensitive to the rate, and the sensitivity grows with the length of the flow. Moving from the 0.5 beta rate to the 1.0 beta rate lowers the value by 8 per cent for a 10-year flow, 16 per cent for 25 years, 23 per cent for 50 years and 29 per cent for a flow that never ends. For a perpetuity the value is one divided by the rate less the growth, so a rate one point lower at 6.35 per cent raises the value by 30 per cent; at the generic setting of the page, a 30-year flow at a weighted cost of 6.90 per cent is worth 15.4 and a point lower is worth 17.3, 12 per cent more. The length of the flow is itself a valuation judgement. Where the cash flow may stop sooner, for example because the equipment is obsolete in ten years, the 10-year line applies: at 6.35 per cent the value is 7.8, not 14.9. This is where the asset-life point of slide 8 enters the discount rate question: the same asset can be worth half as much if its economic life is shorter than the term of the lease.

HOW THE THREE MODELS MEET

A valuation by an investor at a point in time needs a benchmark to say how the asset has done (model 1), a view of how far the reported values can be trusted (model 2) and a rate and a life (model 3). The same quarterly valuation of an unlisted asset is the product of a rate, a life and a lag.

CAUTIONS

The figure is the arithmetic of a growing annuity at generic inputs, not a valuation of any asset. The beta values come from a figure read by eye. The effect of tax and of a time-varying rate (gearing falls over a project financing's life, as the earlier deck's slide on that point says) is ignored.

SOURCE

models_w6.py (value of a growing annuity, checked by direct summation in check_models_w6.py); Van Nieuwerburgh (2026), Figure 3 for the betas; Oxera (2026) for the CMA's method. Interactive page: web/discount.html.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

The life assumed for the cash flows (the lease term, the economic life of the equipment, the residual value) and the sensitivity of the principal's valuation to a one-point change in the rate.

title: Three Models Compared
notes:
THE TABLE

The three models side by side on the questions that matter for a case.

What it corrects. The internal rate of return, for the opportunity cost of the money (Kaplan and Schoar; Gredil, Griffiths and Stucke); the reported risk and return, for the lag in valuations (Getmansky, Lo and Makarov); the price of an asset with no price, through a discount rate (the CMA's determination as the worked case, with Ang, Papanikolaou and Westerfield on illiquidity). Main input. A benchmark and its beta, with the dates of the flows; the weights on past true returns; a comparator beta, gearing and a premium. What can go wrong. A benchmark with the wrong risk or a final value that is the manager's estimate; weights that are not stable or an appraiser who responds to news; a comparator beta that is unstable (the data-centre beta moved from 0.5 to 1.0 in three years) or a premium that is a guess. What the slides show. A PME of 0.80 on one data set and 1.20 on another, and a PME of 1.12 to 1.35 for one fund under three paths of the index; a volatility of 55 per cent of the true figure and a beta of 0.32 for a true 0.80, and an unlisted index with a beta of 0.04; a weighted cost of 6.35 against 8.10 and values 16 per cent apart. A case could test it by. The cash flows and the benchmark of its funds; the quarterly valuations and the transactions that followed them; the rate used in a bid and the comparators behind it.

WHERE THEY ARE WEAK

None of the three is a model of infrastructure. The first needs fully realised funds and a benchmark of the right risk. The second needs weights that stay fixed, and was fitted to hedge funds. The third borrows a beta from listed companies that may not resemble the asset, and the data-centre case shows how much the beta moves. Each is nonetheless a test with a concrete prediction that a portfolio could confirm or contradict: that a fund's verdict changes when its benchmark does; that reported volatility rises when returns are desmoothed; that a valuation changes by a fifth when the beta of its comparators does.

HOW THEY LINK TO THE REST OF THE COURSE

Week 1 has a fee-drag page that quantifies what a fund's fee and carry take from the gross return, and the first model compares what is left with the index. Week 3 covers the J-curve and the evidence of Andonov, Kräussl and Rauh on infrastructure fund returns, which the first model would be used to assess. Week 4 sizes debt and sets cover ratios on a base case that slide 3 shows is biased. Week 5 has the model of search and the dealer, which supplies the theory of the illiquidity premium. Week 7 is about disclosure and supervision, which determines whether valuations can be audited at all.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

For each of the principal's holdings, in one table: the benchmark and beta it reports against, the lag between transactions and valuations, and the discount rate and life behind the value.

title: Case Study: Topic to Be Agreed (Humbert Pang, Gaw Capital)
notes:
AN OUTLINE ONLY

By design this is one slide naming the ground the case covers and leaving the discussion to the guest, Humbert Pang, Managing Principal of Gaw Capital in Hong Kong (his role as the speaker note records it). It states no facts about the case and makes no claim, so it cannot spoil what he says. No case is confirmed for Week 6: the topic is not agreed, and the title says so. He has agreed to serve on the Panel and has the case hour alone, on 26 February 2027. The speaker note records that he was moved from Week 3 on 19 October 2026 and has not yet been told, that he uses WeChat only and that nothing can be sent to him by email. The headings are neutral and could stand over any fund, portfolio or transaction.

WHAT I HAVE NOT CHECKED ABOUT HIS COMPANY

I did not look into Gaw Capital's holdings, funds or reporting practices in this session, and the slide states nothing about them. The case suggestions for Humbert Pang, Justin Chiu and Steven Norris are written separately by the parent session and will rest on checked facts.

KINDS OF CASE THAT FIT THE THREE MODELS, WITHOUT CHOOSING ONE

Model 1 (benchmarking) is tested by any fund or portfolio for which cash flows exist: the contributions and distributions by date, net of fees, and the benchmark the manager and its investors use. A fund that reports an internal rate of return and a multiple, and a second benchmark against which it could be judged, would show how much the verdict depends on the index. Model 2 (smoothing) is tested by any set of assets that are valued between sales: the valuation policy, the valuer and the date of each valuation, and the transactions that followed. A quarterly series of reported values set against sale prices measures the lag directly. Model 3 (the discount rate) is tested by any valuation or bid: the rate, how it was built, the comparators, the gearing assumed, any premium for illiquidity, the life assumed for the cash flows and the residual value. A data-centre or digital-infrastructure asset, if the guest's firm has one, would also test the beta and the useful-life points of slides 7 and 8.

KINDS OF EVIDENCE A GUEST COULD SUPPLY, IN ORDER OF HOW MUCH THEY ADD

A one-page valuation policy: who values, how often, by what method and with what discount rates, and how a valuation is reconciled with a sale price. A quarterly NAV series for a fund or a portfolio over several years. A cash-flow table for a fund, by date and net of fees. The price at which one asset sold, against its last carrying value, and the valuer's discount rate before and after. How investors are told performance, which benchmark they ask for, and what they accept without question. What is public and what may be shown to students and later published in Cities: Global Perspectives, which needs clearance before drafting.

WHAT IS STILL OPEN

The case, the format of the session, whether Pang has been told of the move to Week 6, and the entities. This slide does not propose a topic; the case suggestions are written separately.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

Which of the three models the principal's numbers depend on: the benchmark, the valuation lag and the discount rate and life.

title: Summary
notes:
The same list as the Lecture Outline at the start of the deck, under a different title. There is no thank-you slide (Helen's rule, 2026-10-25): the summary is the last slide.

Run back through it one sentence per item. First-year traffic on new toll roads averaged 0.73 to 0.77 of forecast in four Standard & Poor's studies, so any cover ratio computed on the base case describes a project that is better than the one that is built. The measures of fund performance either ignore the benchmark or depend on it, and the same private equity funds are shown to beat or lag the index depending on the data and the index: 0.80 on Venture Economics data, 1.20 on Burgiss buyout cash flows, 1.07 against small-cap value. Regulators with the same method, the same companies and the same year arrive at weighted costs of capital from 4.03 to 4.29 per cent for water, through different betas, risk-free rates and dates. A data-centre beta moved from about 0.5 to about 1 in three years, and two hyperscalers moved the lives of their servers in opposite directions in the same year. The three models then give three tests of a number for an asset that does not trade: whether the fund beat the index, which depends on its timing and the benchmark's beta (1.12 to 1.35 for one fund); whether reported risk can be believed, since values that lag prices cut volatility to 55 per cent of the truth and the beta to 0.32 for a true 0.80; and what the discount rate does, a difference of 16 per cent in value between two plausible betas for a 25-year flow. Then the case, where the guest tells us what the numbers behind a real portfolio rest on.
